title: John Wesley
wiki_lead:
John Wesley (; 28 June [O.S. 17 June] 1703 – 2 March 1791) was an English cleric, theologian, and evangelist who was a principal leader of a revival movement within the Church of England known as Methodism. The societies he founded became the dominant form of the ongoing independent Methodist movement.
Educated at Charterhouse and Christ Church, Oxford, Wesley was elected a fellow of Lincoln College, Oxford, in 1726 and ordained as an Anglican priest two years later. At Oxford, he led the "Holy Club", a society formed for the purpose of the study and the pursuit of a devout Christian life. After an unsuccessful two-year ministry in Savannah, Georgia, he returned to London and joined a religious society led by Moravian Christians. On 24 May 1738, he experienced what has come to be called his evangelical conversion. He left the Moravians and began his own ministry.
A key step in the development of Wesley's ministry was to travel widely and preach outdoors, embracing Arminian doctrines. Moving across Great Britain and Ireland, he helped form and organise small Christian groups that developed intensive and personal accountability, discipleship, and religious instruction. He appointed itinerant, unordained evangelists—both women and men—to care for these groups of people. Under Wesley's direction, Methodists became leaders in many social issues of the day, including the abolition of slavery and support for women preachers.
Although he was not a systematic theologian, Wesley argued against Calvinism and for the notion of Christian perfection, which he cited as the reason that he felt God "raised up" Methodists into existence. His evangelicalism, firmly grounded in sacramental theology, maintained that means of grace played a role in sanctification of the believer; however, he taught that it was by faith a believer was transformed into the likeness of Christ. He held that, in this life, Christians could achieve a state where the love of God "reigned supreme in their hearts", giving them not only outward but inward holiness. Wesley's teachings, collectively known as Wesleyan theology, continue to inform the doctrine of Methodist churches. In his early ministry years, Wesley was barred from preaching in many parish churches and the Methodists were persecuted; he later became widely respected, and by the end of his life, was described as "the best-loved man in England".

Early life
John Wesley was born on 28 June [O.S. 17 June] 1703 in Epworth, 23 miles (37 km) north-west of Lincoln. He was the 15th child of Samuel Wesley and his wife Susanna Wesley (née Annesley). Samuel Wesley was a graduate of the University of Oxford and a poet who, from 1696, was rector of Epworth. He married Susanna, the 25th child of Samuel Annesley, a dissenting minister, in 1689. Ultimately, she bore 19 children, nine of whom lived beyond infancy. She and Samuel Wesley had become members of the Church of England as young adults.

John Wesley's ancestry can be traced back to 14th-century England. The Wesley family was considered one of high respectability in southern England. In almost every generation there existed an eminent clergyman and accomplished scholar. The paternal grandfather of John and Charles Wesley was John Westley (1636–1678), an English dissenting minister, who was ordained in 1658 (the year of Oliver Cromwell's death) at Whitchurch, a small market town in Shropshire. At this time the Commonwealth had been vanquished, and with the re-establishment of the throne and the episcopal form of church government, Westley was regarded as one of Cromwell's Puritans. Subsequently, he was arrested by the State Church officers, and carried to prison at Blandford. Because of his amiable character and gentle nature, his sentence was commuted and was allowed to return to his parish.

grok_lead: John Wesley (17 June 1703 â 2 March 1791) was an English Anglican cleric and theologian who founded the Methodist movement within the Church of England, sparking the 18th-century Evangelical Revival through emphasis on personal conversion, methodical discipline in faith, and open-air preaching. Born in Epworth, Lincolnshire, to Anglican parents Samuel and Susanna Wesley, he received early education at Charterhouse School before entering Christ Church, Oxford, in 1720, where he later became a fellow of Lincoln College. At Oxford, Wesley led the Holy Club, a group focused on rigorous spiritual practices including regular communion, fasting, and visiting prisoners, which earned them the nickname "Methodists" for their systematic approach to piety. Ordained as a priest in 1728, he initially sought personal assurance of salvation through works but experienced a transformative spiritual awakening on 24 May 1738 at a meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, where he felt his "heart strangely warmed," assuring him of forgiveness through faith. Wesley's mission to the colony of Georgia from 1735 to 1738, intended to evangelize settlers and Native Americans, ended in failure due to personal conflicts and his rigid high-church views, prompting his return to England and shift toward evangelical preaching. Influenced by Moravian pietism encountered during the voyage, he began field preaching in 1739 after being denied pulpits, addressing crowds outdoors and facing mob violence, such as the Wednesbury riots, while organizing converts into disciplined societies and classes for accountability and mutual support. Over five decades, he traveled approximately 250,000 miles on horseback across Britain, preaching an estimated 40,000 sermons and establishing a network of circuits and annual conferences that structured Methodism's growth, reaching 71,668 members in Britain by his death. Despite remaining an Anglican and opposing separation until late in life, Wesley's authorization of lay preachers and ordinations, including for American Methodists in 1784, laid the groundwork for Methodism's independence as a denomination. His teachings on Arminian theology, Christian perfection, and social holiness addressed doctrinal controversies like Calvinism and promoted reforms against slavery and for education, contributing to moral and societal renewal amid industrial upheavals. Wesley's prolific writings, including sermons, journals, and hymns composed with his brother Charles, provided doctrinal standards that defined Methodist identity and influenced global evangelicalism.
